analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to count the dollar cost of carbon, methane, and nitrous oxide pollution in regulations and purchasing decisions.
analysis.headline: Fourteen Senate Democrats sponsored the bill, but it never moved past the Environment and Public Works Committee, dying without a vote when the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every federal agency, when writing major regulations or making big purchasing decisions, to calculate and document the economic damage caused by the carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide emissions involved. It writes a table of per-ton pollution costs into law — for example, about $42 per ton of carbon dioxide in 2020 at a central estimate — and creates two scientific bodies to update those numbers at least every five years. This would make the hidden costs of pollution visible in official decisions, including the damage from floods, crop losses, and health effects.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people benefit because government decisions would have to account for the real costs of climate pollution — crop damage, flood risk, health effects, and disaster spending that taxpayers currently absorb. Communities living near polluting facilities would get clearer documentation of the harms considered, and future generations benefit from rules that weigh long-term climate damage instead of treating it as free.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities exposed to pollution

how_it_helps.text: Agencies writing major rules and making substantial procurement decisions must consider and document the cost of carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide, using the per-ton dollar values written into the bill.

The bill counts climate damage as including harm to agriculture, energy use, human health, and property damage from increased flood risk and sea level rise, so these costs appear in official analyses.

An interagency working group must re-evaluate the pollution-cost method at least every five years, with public comment and input from industry groups, and a 10-member scientific review committee selected by the National Academies of Sciences advises on updates.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers and other large emitters would bear higher documented costs in regulatory analyses, making rules that restrict their emissions easier to justify and harder to dismiss. Federal purchasing would also have to factor in pollution costs, which could raise the upfront cost of some government contracts. Consumers could eventually see some compliance costs passed through in energy prices, though the bill sets no tax or fee directly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and large emitters

drawbacks.text: The bill hardcodes dollar-per-ton tables into statute through 2050, which could leave outdated or contested values in force until the working group completes a revision cycle, and disputes over which discount rate to use (the bill requires several, from 5% to a high-impact 3% estimate) can swing the numbers dramatically — from about $12 to $123 per ton of carbon dioxide in 2020.

Counting pollution costs in regulatory analyses and procurement raises the documented cost of energy and infrastructure decisions, and critics argue such costs can be passed to consumers through higher prices even though the bill imposes no tax or fee directly.

The bill uses damage estimates that reflect global climate harms, not just harms to the United States, which supporters call appropriate for a global problem but which critics see as inflating the cost figures applied to domestic decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but indirect: this is an accounting and transparency requirement, not a tax, so its main effect is forcing the government to stop treating climate damage as free when it writes rules and buys goods. The costs are mostly borne by emitters through stronger, better-documented regulations, with some risk of pass-through to energy consumers and a genuine design weakness in statutorily freezing the numbers. On balance, the bill's core function — making pollution costs visible in official decisions — outweighs those costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Michael Bennet introduced the Pollution Transparency Act on October 5, 2017, joined by 13 Democratic cosponsors including Senators Feinstein, Harris, Warren, and Whitehouse.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and other large emitters are better off, since agencies never had to document the dollar cost of their pollution in rulemaking and procurement decisions. The Senate committee leadership that declined to act also avoided a vote on the issue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Polluting industries and the committee that stalled it

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Pollution Transparency Act on October 5, 2017.

for.name: 13 Democratic senators
for.role: Cosponsors (Feinstein, Harris, Wyden, Whitehouse, Hassan, Cardin, Merkley, Murray, Van Hollen, Warren, Heinrich, Hirono, Udall)

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. John Barrasso (R-WY)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remaining 15 months of the Congress.

against.name: President Donald Trump
against.what_they_did: Earlier in 2017, disbanded the existing interagency working group on the social cost of greenhouse gases and ordered agencies to discount climate costs, the approach this bill would have overridden by statute.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired Environment and Public Works Committee never scheduled action.

industries.note: Rules restricting coal, oil, and gas emissions would rest on documented damage costs — up to roughly $123 per ton of carbon dioxide in 2020 at the high-impact estimate — instead of treating emissions as free. The industry's gain from the bill's failure is the public's continued absorption of climate damage costs.

industries.industry: Federal contractors and energy suppliers to government
industries.note: Agencies making substantial procurement decisions would have to factor in the cost of emissions from purchases, which could shift federal buying toward lower-pollution options and raise the bar for high-emission suppliers.
